Article.ArticleTitle: Acute lysyl oxidase inhibition alters microvascular function in normotensive, but not hypertensive, men and women.

Abstract.AbstractText: The Lysyl oxidase (LOX) family of enzymes regulates collagen cross-linking. LOX is upregulated in hypertension, increasing vascular stiffness. In vivo human research is sparse as long-term LOX inhibition in animals causes vascular instability. Our aim was to evaluate the effects of LOX inhibition on cutaneous microvascular function to determine if LOX function was upregulated in hypertensive humans. Four intradermal microdialysis fibers were placed in the forearm of 10 young (age: 24±1 y, MAP: 87±2 mmHg), 10 normotensive (age: 50±2 y, MAP: 84±1 mmHg), and 10 hypertensive (age: 53±2 y, MAP 112±2 mmHg) subjects. Two sites were perfused with 10 mM β-aminopropionitrile (BAPN) to inhibit LOX. The remaining two sites were perfused with lactated Ringer's (control). A norepinephrine dose response (NE: 10-12-10-2 M) was performed to examine receptor-mediated vasoconstrictor function. A sodium nitroprusside dose response (SNP: 10-8-10-1.3 M) was performed to examine vascular smooth muscle vasodilator function. Red cell flux was measured via laser Doppler flowmetry and normalized to cutaneous vascular conductance (CVC: flux∙MAP-1). LogEC50's were calculated to determine changes in vaso-sensitivity. Skin tissue samples were analyzed for both extracellular matrix-bound and soluble LOX. LOX inhibition augmented vasoconstrictor sensitivity in the young (control: -6.0, BAPN: -7.1; p=0.03) and normotensive (control: -4.8, BAPN: -7.0; p=0.01), but not hypertensive (control: -6.0, BAPN: -6.1; p=0.79), men and women. Relative to young, extracellular matrix-bound LOX expression was higher in the hypertensive subjects (young: 100±8, hypertensive: 162±8; p=0.002). These results suggest that upregulated LOX may contribute to vascular stiffness and microvascular dysfunction characteristic in hypertension.
